sources.title: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017)

blocks.text: One attention computation mixes the values of all tokens with a single set of weights. A token may need to look at one token for grammar and at another for meaning at the same time. **Multi-head attention** runs several attention computations side by side. Each one has its own part of every vector. Then it joins the results.
The numbers in this lesson are small invented values chosen so that you can follow the arithmetic. They are not learned from data and they do not show real language relationships.

Implement the multi-head attention mechanism, a critical component of transformer models. Given Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) matrices, compute the attention outputs for multiple heads and concatenate the results.

`multi_head_attention(Q, K, V, n_heads)` takes **already projected** matrices `Q`, `K`, `V` with shape `(T, d_model)`. It requires `d_model % n_heads == 0`. It returns shape `(T, d_model)`. `compute_qkv(X, W_q, W_k, W_v)` makes the projections. There is no mask and no output projection in this question.
blocks.title: Inputs and output

items: [[article:scaled-dot-product-attention|Scaled dot-product attention]]: scores, softmax, and the weighted sum.
[[article:arrays-and-shapes|Array shapes]]: `reshape` and `transpose` for the head split.

blocks.text: We use three tokens, a model width of 4, and 2 heads, so each head has width 2. Switch the head to see that the heads compare different things. Select a token or a number to trace it.

blocks.latex: Q = XW_Q,\quad K = XW_K,\quad V = XW_V

items: $Q_h$ is the slice of $Q$ with columns $h d_k$ to $(h+1) d_k - 1$.
Every head has $T \times T$ scores. For $H$ heads the scores have shape $(H, T, T)$.
The total work is about the same as one head of width $d_{\text{model}}$, because each head is smaller.

blocks.text: Choose the head width and switch the scaling on or off. The vectors are fixed random numbers with mean 0 and variance 1. Without scaling, the score spread grows with the width. The softmax becomes sharp: one weight near 1.
The head split is easy to get wrong because the wrong version runs without an error. Choose a version and compare its first head with the correct one.
A wrong reshape keeps the shape and changes the meaning. Check one head against a plain slice `Q[:, :d_k]`.
blocks.title: A silent bug

blocks.text: If `d_model` is not divisible by `n_heads`, the supplied function raises ValueError. A model width of 6 with 4 heads cannot be split.

notes.text: Project the same input into queries, keys, and values with separate weights.
Scale dot products by the square root of the per-head width.
Subtract each row maximum before exponentiation to keep softmax stable.
Weight the value vectors by the attention probabilities.
Require a positive head count that divides the model width.
Reshape into heads and move the head axis to the front.
A batched matrix product evaluates independent attention for all heads.
Move the head axis back and combine features into the model width.

lesson-q316-multi-head-attention/multi-h.alt_text: Multi-head attention flow from token projections through scores, softmax, weighted values, head concatenation, and output.
lesson-q316-multi-head-attention/multi-h.description: The static diagram preserves the complete information path when animation is disabled.

count-heads.prompt: `d_model` is 512 and `n_heads` is 8. What is the width of each head?

explanation.default: Divide the model width by the number of heads.

explain-heads.prompt: In your own words: what does each head see, and why do the heads give different attention weights?

explanation.correct: Each head sees all tokens but only its own slice of every query, key, and value vector. The slices come from different columns of the projection matrices, so each head compares tokens in a different way and produces different weights. Concatenation puts the head results side by side.

new-weight.prompt: A single head has width 1. The query is [1]. The keys are [0] and [1.0986]. The values are [10] and [20]. What is the attention output? (Round to one decimal.)

explanation.correct: The scores are 0 and 1.0986, with $\sqrt{d_k} = 1$. Softmax gives weights 0.25 and 0.75 because $e^{1.0986} = 3$. The output is $0.25 \cdot 10 + 0.75 \cdot 20 = 17.5$.
explanation.default: Compute the two scores, take softmax to get the weights, then mix the values.

wrong.15: That is the plain average. The second key has the larger score, so it gets the larger weight.
wrong.20: That would need weight 1 on the second value. The weights are 0.25 and 0.75.

predict-shape.prompt: `Q` has shape (3, 4) and `n_heads` is 2. What is the shape of `Q.reshape(3, 2, 2).transpose(1, 0, 2)`?

explanation.correct: The reshape gives (3, 2, 2) = (T, H, d_k). The transpose moves the head axis first: (2, 3, 2) = (H, T, d_k).
explanation.default: `transpose(1, 0, 2)` swaps the first two axes of (T, H, d_k).

wrong.(3, 2, 2): That is the shape before the transpose.
wrong.(3, 4): That is the shape of Q. The split adds a head axis.

checks.name: one head equals plain attention
checks.code:
Q = np.array([[1., 0.], [0., 1.]]); K = Q.copy(); V = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
s = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(2); w = np.exp(s - s.max(1, keepdims=True)); w /= w.sum(1, keepdims=True)
assert np.allclose(multi_head_attention(Q, K, V, 1), w @ V)
